items.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Lionel called me. And he says, “hey Gates” he says, “Louis gave me the record, you’ve got to play in my band,” he says, “he tells me you play drums also.”

ctx.x: Yeah, absolutely. Tell me about what possessed you to try to get your Dream Band going? The big band?

That was just a fluke. It was the biggest fluke. I recorded a band in New York in 1956 or something like that and I was sick because it wasn’t good — not to me, it wasn’t good. I used the same rhythm section that was with my little group. I always try to use the guys who travel with me and kill themselves on the road, to give them a good job. If I did a T.V. show, I was steadily using a quartet, three of the guys from the house band, I want my guys on there. I always tried to push them on there. So I put them on…

idea was I was going to hire six different arrangers and pay tribute to six different band leaders, like Duke Ellington, Lionel Hampton, Count Basie, Tommy Dorsey, Benny Goodman and Artie Shaw. And I was going to take something out of each arrangement, like Artie Shaw’s clarinet chorus on “Stardust” just the first 16 bars, and somewhere would sneak it in the arrangement, or part of Ben Webster’s chorus on “Cottontail,” whatever, you know. items.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 5, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: But we were the first two so there was Lionel Hampton and Red Norvo, so maybe — I’m not sure, but Leonard saw it like that.

ctx.x: So I’m going to read — this is the Leonard Feather Encyclopedia of Jazz from 1960. And one Terry Gibbs, even back then, had an entry in it, and at the end it says, “Gibbs has always played with tremendous vitality and a natural beat that established him as the bop era’s equivalent of Lionel Hampton.”

Well I don’t know what he means. I don’t know what he means by that. I think maybe popularity or something, because Milt Jackson and I were the only two vibes players on the scene at the time who got well known as vibes players until Teddy Charles and Joe Roland, and another whole bunch of musicians. But we were the first two so there was Lionel Hampton and Red Norvo, so maybe — I’m not sure, but Leonard saw it like that.
I think that he wanted to make a distinction between the styles and the fact that you embraced bebop as a musical language and were able to play it on the vibes. I’m assuming that’s his point.
